slides.title: Why 180 days?
slides.text: A muscle doesn't get stronger in a few days. In the first weeks your brain learns to find the muscle and use it alone; the muscle really strengthens at 8–12 weeks. Guidelines recommend at least 3 months. Six months lets the strength settle and the habit stick.
slides.imageAlt: A foot climbing bright steps

slides.title: What changes, what's coming?
slides.text: The plan is split into six 30-day months; the last week of each is light. Along the way you learn 7 moves: Slow Squeeze, Step Squeeze, Step Release, Double Peak, Quick Half Squeeze, Half Long Hold and Wave. Your control gets finer and your endurance grows.
slides.imageAlt: A spiral staircase seen from above

slides.text: A strong, well-controlled pelvic floor can help reduce dribbling after urinating and leaking when you cough, help keep an erection and help you control ejaculation. It is also often recommended after prostate surgery.
slides.imageAlt: A country road at sunrise with someone running

slides.title: What did people experience?
slides.text: In men with erection problems, after 6 months of exercise 40% regained normal erections and 35.5% improved clearly. Of 40 men with premature ejaculation, 33 (82.5%) gained control within 12 weeks. About three in four men with dribbling after urinating no longer had it after 6 months.
slides.imageAlt: Stones balanced on pebbles

quiz.question: How long does it usually take the pelvic floor muscle to get stronger?
options: It starts in the first weeks; the real difference comes over months
quiz.explain: You learn to use the muscle correctly in the first weeks; a clear gain in strength takes 2–3 months. The good results in studies also came from regular 3–6 month programmes. That is why the plan is 180 days.

slides.imageAlt: An alarm clock on a wooden floor

slides.title: Your roadmap is ready
slides.text: Which day of the plan you're on, what this week holds, when the next move comes: it's all on the roadmap.
slides.imageAlt: Two feet standing on a gravel path

items: Muscles get stronger over months, not days; that is why the plan is 180 days.
Over six months you learn 7 moves and build control and endurance step by step.
In studies, most men who trained regularly saw better erections, ejaculation control and less dribbling.

slides.title: An invisible hammock
slides.text: The pelvic floor is a set of muscles stretched like a hammock beneath the pelvis. It carries the bladder and bowel and helps you hold in urine and wind. During an erection it presses on the base of the penis to help keep it firm, and it contributes to ejaculation with its rhythmic contractions.
slides.imageAlt: An empty hammock strung between two trees in a misty garden

slides.title: What happens when it weakens?
slides.text: Common signs: a few drops coming out after urinating (post-micturition dribble) and leaking a little urine when coughing, sneezing or lifting something heavy. Age, long sitting, a chronic cough, excess weight and prostate surgery can affect these muscles.
slides.imageAlt: An old brass tap dripping in a park

slides.myth: Kegel exercises are only for women.
slides.fact: Men have the same muscles, and they can be trained. Mayo Clinic notes that Kegel exercises can help bladder control in men. They're also often recommended after prostate surgery.
slides.imageAlt: An older man exercising on a yoga mat in a bright room

quiz.question: Which can help reduce dribbling after urinating?
options: Squeezing the pelvic floor muscle a few times after urinating
Drinking less water during the day
Stopping the flow now and then while urinating
quiz.explain: Squeezing the muscle pushes out the last drops left in the urethra. In a small study of 55 men, about three quarters of the participants had no more dribbling after 6 months of exercises that included this move. Drinking less water, on the other hand, concentrates the urine.

slides.imageAlt: A plain, clean bathroom sink with grey tiles

slides.title: Find the muscle
slides.text: In the short lesson you'll see step by step how to find your pelvic floor muscle and how to work it without tensing your belly or glutes.
slides.imageAlt: A man lying on his back resting in a sunny meadow

items: If you see blood in your urine
If you have pain or burning when urinating or in your groin
If urine leaking or erection problems started suddenly
If your urine flow has become markedly weaker or you feel you can't empty your bladder fully
slides.imageAlt: A stethoscope lying on a wooden table

items: The pelvic floor is a muscle group that plays a role in urinary control and sexual function.
Dribbling after urinating and leaking when coughing are common signs of weakness.
It can get stronger with regular, correct exercise; the difference usually shows within a few months.

slides.title: 1–2: Breathing and the wrong muscles
slides.text: Don't hold your breath while squeezing; keep breathing. Keep your belly, glutes and legs relaxed. When you use the right muscle, almost nothing shows from the outside; the feeling is inside, like your testicles being drawn up slightly.
slides.imageAlt: A man outdoors lifting his head and taking a deep breath, side view

slides.title: 3–4: Relaxing and overdoing it
slides.text: After every squeeze, relax the muscle completely for at least as long as you squeezed; relaxing is part of the exercise. More reps don't mean faster results: a tired muscle works incorrectly. Stick to the number of reps in the programme.
slides.imageAlt: Hands resting loosely on a knee on a bench

slides.title: 5: Exercising while urinating
slides.text: Stopping your urine flow can be tried once to find the muscle, but don't do it as an exercise. If it becomes a habit, it can interfere with the bladder emptying fully. Do your exercises outside the toilet, at a relaxed moment.
slides.imageAlt: A toilet sign in a plain corridor, without text

slides.myth: The more I squeeze, the faster I'll get stronger.
slides.fact: Like other muscles, the pelvic floor gets stronger while resting. Too many reps lead to fatigue and using the wrong muscles. Training regularly, correctly and in moderation gives better results.
slides.imageAlt: A tired man wiping his sweat with a towel after exercise

quiz.question: What is the most important step after a contraction?
options: Going straight into the next contraction
quiz.explain: Relaxing lets the muscle rest and get ready for the next contraction. Skipping the relaxation tires the muscle; holding your breath also increases pressure inside the abdomen.

slides.imageAlt: A calm water surface in evening light

slides.title: A set with the right breathing
slides.text: In today's workout, focus on breathing out as you squeeze and breathing in as you relax. Put one hand on your belly; it should hardly move.
slides.imageAlt: A man sitting on a mat breathing with his hand on his chest

items: Keep breathing while you squeeze; keep your belly, glutes and legs relaxed.
Relax the muscle completely after every squeeze.
Don't exercise while urinating, and stick to the number of reps in the programme.

slides.title: An erection is about blood flow
slides.text: When you're aroused, the blood vessels in the penis widen and the spongy tissue fills with blood. For this, the blood vessels need to be flexible and healthy. Because the penis's blood vessels are very narrow, they can show damage to blood vessel health early.
slides.imageAlt: An aerial shot of river channels branching like the limbs of a tree

slides.title: Risk factors
slides.text: Smoking, high blood pressure, diabetes, high cholesterol, excess weight and inactivity wear down blood vessels. Most of these can be changed: movement, nutrition and quitting smoking are good for both your heart and your erections.
slides.imageAlt: A blood pressure monitor strapped to an arm on a table

slides.text: The American Urological Association notes that erection problems can be a warning sign of cardiovascular disease. In some studies, this problem appeared a few years before events such as a heart attack.
slides.imageAlt: Hands looking at a smartwatch on a wrist

quiz.question: Which is a risk factor that affects erections and can be changed?
quiz.explain: Smoking narrows blood vessels and wears down their inner lining. Quitting, moving and keeping your blood pressure and blood sugar under control support blood vessel health.

slides.imageAlt: Hands tying a running shoe on the asphalt

slides.title: Go for a walk today
slides.text: Plan a 20–30 minute brisk walk and put it in your calendar. Regular movement supports the flexibility of your blood vessels; you can aim for 150 minutes a week in total.
slides.imageAlt: Someone walking down a tree-lined path in autumn, from behind

items: If erection problems started suddenly or keep coming back
If you have chest pain, shortness of breath or palpitations
If you haven't had your blood pressure, blood sugar or cholesterol checked in a long time
If you have pain in the penis or a marked curve
slides.imageAlt: A hand taking notes at a doctor's desk, no face

items: An erection depends on healthy, flexible blood vessels.
Erection problems can be an early warning for cardiovascular health.
Quitting smoking, movement and healthy eating protect both at once.

slides.title: Two types of leaking
slides.text: Stress type: leaking a small amount when coughing, sneezing or lifting something heavy. Urge type: a sudden, strong need to go and not making it in time. Both can happen together; pelvic floor exercises support both.
slides.imageAlt: A man carrying a heavy box on the stairs

slides.title: When a sudden urge comes
slides.text: Don't rush; stop where you are or sit down. Quickly squeeze and release your pelvic floor muscle a few times. Breathe calmly and turn your attention to something else. When the urge fades, walk slowly to the toilet.
slides.imageAlt: A man stopping to catch his breath at the edge of a pavement

slides.myth: If I drink less water, I won't leak.
slides.fact: Drinking less water concentrates the urine and can irritate the bladder; this can make urgency worse. Drinking enough, evenly through the day, is better for the bladder.
slides.imageAlt: A hand filling a glass with water at a table

quiz.question: What is the first step when a sudden urge to go comes?
options: Stopping and doing a few quick contractions
Rushing to the toilet straight away
quiz.explain: Rushing and panicking can make the urge stronger. Stopping, a few quick contractions and calm breathing help the urge pass; then you can walk calmly.

slides.imageAlt: A man sitting on a bench at sunset, from behind

slides.title: Try it at the next sudden urge
slides.text: Next time a sudden urge comes, instead of rushing, stop, do 3–5 quick contractions and wait for the urge to ease. Notice how many seconds it takes to pass.
slides.imageAlt: Two feet standing on a gravel path

items: If you see blood in your urine
If you have burning, pain or a fever when urinating
If leaking started suddenly or keeps getting worse
If you have difficulty urinating or feel your bladder doesn't empty fully
slides.imageAlt: Two empty chairs by a window in a clinic

items: Leaking can be of the stress or the urge type.
Don't rush when a sudden urge comes: stop, do quick contractions, breathe calmly.
Drinking less water isn't the answer; drinking evenly is good for the bladder.

sources.title: NHS – Urinary incontinence

slides.title: Choose the right time
slides.text: Don't have this conversation in bed or right after a difficult moment. Choose a time when you're both calm and unhurried: a walk, a coffee. Starting small is fine too; you don't need to solve everything in one conversation.
slides.imageAlt: A couple walking hand in hand on the beach at sunset, from behind

slides.title: Speak in "I" statements
slides.text: Instead of blaming, describe your own feelings: something like “I've been feeling tense lately.” An example opening: “I want to talk to you about something important, because I care about us.” This sentence turns the conversation into teamwork.
slides.imageAlt: Two cups of coffee and hands facing each other on a wooden table

slides.title: Listening is part of talking
slides.text: Ask your partner what they think and listen without interrupting. They may have worries or questions too. Repeating what you heard in your own words makes them feel understood.
slides.imageAlt: An older man listening attentively, side view

slides.text: The International Society for Sexual Medicine (ISSM) notes that couples may avoid this topic out of embarrassment or fear of hurting each other, and that this can reduce closeness. Even if talking feels strange, it's often a relief.
slides.imageAlt: A couple sitting side by side at a window, from behind

quiz.question: What is the best moment for this conversation?
options: A moment when you're both calm
Right after a difficult moment, in bed
In the middle of an argument
quiz.explain: Talking at a calm moment makes getting defensive less likely. Things said in tense moments are more easily misunderstood.

slides.imageAlt: Two chairs on a balcony by the sea

slides.title: Write your own opening sentence
slides.text: On your phone or a piece of paper, write the first sentence you want to say to your partner: in your own words, with "I" statements, and short. When you're ready, start with that sentence.
slides.imageAlt: Hands writing a note on a phone

items: Choose a calm, unhurried moment; not in bed or during an argument.
Describe your own feelings with "I" statements instead of blaming.
Listening is half of talking; ask what they think too.

sources.title: ISSM – How does erectile dysfunction impact sexual partners?
ISSM – How can I manage performance anxiety and psychogenic ED?
NHS – Erection problems (erectile dysfunction)

slides.title: A very common situation
slides.text: Having an erection problem now and then is very common and usually nothing to worry about. Stress, tiredness and anxiety are among the most common causes. It's not a measure of strength or manhood.
slides.imageAlt: Blurred people walking through a busy square

slides.title: The anxiety cycle
slides.text: When you worry, your body releases stress hormones; these can reduce blood flow and make an erection harder. When there's difficulty, worry about the next time grows and the cycle feeds itself. To break the cycle, move your attention from the outcome to your senses and reduce the pressure.
slides.imageAlt: A spiral staircase photographed from above

slides.myth: It happened once, so it'll always happen.
slides.fact: One-off or occasional difficulties are very common and don't predict the future. Anxiety-related erection problems can be managed: talking, reducing pressure and, if needed, working with a professional help.
slides.imageAlt: A rainbow among the clouds after rain

quiz.question: What helps most to break the anxiety cycle?
options: Paying attention to your senses instead of performance
Trying never to think about it
quiz.explain: Pushing yourself and trying to suppress the thought often increase anxiety. Paying attention to touch, warmth and breath reduces pressure. The "sensate focus" exercises used by sex therapists are also based on this idea.

slides.imageAlt: The silhouette of a man breathing in front of a curtain

slides.title: 2 minutes of slow breathing
slides.text: Now, or before getting close, breathe slowly for a few minutes; make the out-breath a little longer than the in-breath. The aim isn't to force an erection but to calm your body.
slides.imageAlt: A calm sea and horizon in morning light

items: If the problem has been coming back often for a few weeks
If you also don't get erections in the morning or when you're alone
If there's pain, a curve or another new symptom
If anxiety or low mood affects your daily life
slides.imageAlt: Two armchairs facing each other in an empty room

items: Occasional erection problems are common and usually temporary.
Anxiety can set up a self-feeding cycle by reducing blood flow.
Paying attention to your senses, reducing pressure and slow breathing help break the cycle.

sources.title: NHS – Erection problems (erectile dysfunction)
ISSM – How can I manage performance anxiety and psychogenic erectile dysfunction (ED)?

slides.title: There are many ways to be close
slides.text: Hugging, holding hands, laughing together and talking are also intimacy. Sex is just one of them. These small moments nourish a sense of trust and connection.
slides.imageAlt: A couple cooking together in the kitchen and laughing

slides.title: Sensate focus
slides.text: In this method used in sex therapy, partners take turns touching each other. The aim isn't arousal but noticing warmth, texture and pressure. In the first stages, the genitals aren't touched, so the pressure to “perform” eases.
slides.imageAlt: Two hands touching, close-up

slides.title: Less pressure, more closeness
slides.text: Knowing that not every moment of closeness has to end a certain way is a relief. When expectations drop, the body relaxes more easily too; that's good for erections and pleasure as well.
slides.imageAlt: Two cups on a tray on a blanket in bed

slides.fact: Intimacy also includes touching, talking and spending time together. The ISSM notes that even without an erection, couples can stay close by hugging, kissing and touching.
slides.imageAlt: A couple walking side by side in a park in autumn, from behind

quiz.question: What is the aim of the sensate focus exercise?
options: Getting aroused as fast as possible
quiz.explain: This method was developed to reduce anticipatory anxiety. Attention goes to the senses in the moment, not to the outcome.

slides.imageAlt: Hands reaching towards each other in warm light

slides.title: 20 minutes without phones
slides.text: This week, leave your phones in another room and spend 20 minutes together with your partner: a walk, a meal or just talking. You don't have to achieve anything.
slides.imageAlt: Playing cards and dice on a table

items: Intimacy also includes touching, talking and spending time together.
Sensate focus is a sex therapy method that reduces pressure.
As expectations drop, both the body and the relationship relax.

sources.title: SMSNA – What is sensate focus and how does it work?
ISSM – How does erectile dysfunction impact sexual partners?
WHO – Sexual health

slides.title: How much fluid?
slides.text: The NHS recommends about 6–8 glasses of fluid a day. Water, milk and sugar-free drinks all count. You may need more in hot weather, when exercising or when you're ill.
slides.imageAlt: A glass jug full of water and a glass on a table

slides.title: Check with your urine colour
slides.text: Pale straw-coloured urine usually shows you're getting enough fluid. Dark yellow, strong-smelling urine can be a sign you need to drink more. Drinking too little concentrates the urine and can irritate the bladder.
slides.imageAlt: A glass of water with a slice of lemon by a window

slides.title: Caffeine and fizzy drinks
slides.text: Coffee, tea, cola and fizzy drinks can make urgency worse for some people. You don't need to give them all up; cut down and notice the difference. Spreading your drinks across the day is better than drinking a lot at once.
slides.imageAlt: A cup of Turkish coffee on a wooden tray with a glass of water beside it

slides.text: Concentrated urine can irritate the bladder wall and cause a frequent need to go. That's why, with bladder problems, drinking evenly rather than cutting back on fluids is usually recommended.
slides.imageAlt: Water droplets on a glass surface, close-up

quiz.question: What's the easiest way to tell you're getting enough fluid?
options: Going to the toilet once a day
quiz.explain: Urine colour is a practical indicator. Thirst sometimes comes late; going to the toilet very rarely can also show you're getting too little fluid.

slides.imageAlt: A man walking with a water bottle in the side pocket of his backpack, from behind

slides.title: Set yourself a water reminder
slides.text: Add 3–4 water reminders during the day to your phone's clock or calendar. Putting a bottle of water on your desk also helps.
slides.imageAlt: A notebook and a reusable water bottle on a desk

items: Aim for about 6–8 glasses of fluid a day; more in the heat and during sport.
Pale straw-coloured urine is a good sign.
Caffeine and fizzy drinks can make urgency worse for some people.

sources.title: NHS – Water, drinks and hydration
NHS – Urinary incontinence
Gloucestershire Hospitals NHS – Fluid and caffeine intake for bladder and bowel health

slides.title: Eating for your blood vessels
slides.text: A Mediterranean-style diet rich in vegetables, fruit, whole grains, pulses, fish and olive oil supports heart and blood vessel health. When your blood vessels are healthy, the blood flow needed for an erection is supported too.
slides.imageAlt: A bowl full of pulses and vegetables on a wooden table

slides.title: The plate model
slides.text: Fill half your plate with vegetables and salad, a quarter with a protein such as fish, chicken or pulses, and the remaining quarter with a whole grain such as bulgur, wholemeal bread or brown rice. Add a portion of fruit on the side.
slides.imageAlt: A plate half full of vegetables, from above

slides.text: In a study of 65 men with metabolic syndrome, erectile function improved more in the group that ate a Mediterranean-style diet for 2 years than in the control group. In another study of obese men, weight loss and movement improved sexual function in about a third of participants.
slides.imageAlt: A Mediterranean table with vegetables, outdoors

quiz.question: According to the plate model, what should half the plate be filled with?
quiz.explain: Vegetables provide fibre, vitamins and minerals and keep you full. Protein and whole grains share the other half of the plate.

slides.imageAlt: A colourful salad bowl on a wooden table

slides.title: Make one meal using the plate model
slides.text: This week, make at least one meal using the plate model: half vegetables, a quarter protein, a quarter whole grains. If you like, take a photo of your plate to track yourself.
slides.imageAlt: Hands slicing cucumber on a board

items: A Mediterranean-style diet supports blood vessel health.
The plate model: half vegetables, a quarter protein, a quarter whole grains.
Losing weight and moving can also help sexual function.

slides.title: In the short term
slides.text: Alcohol slows down the nervous system; it can make arousal, erections and ejaculation harder. It also disrupts sleep: even though it makes falling asleep easier, it can break up sleep in the second half of the night.
slides.imageAlt: A dim bedroom and a window at night

slides.title: In the long term
slides.text: Regular heavy drinking raises blood pressure, strains the liver and can affect hormone balance. Over time these harm blood vessel health and sexual function. According to the World Health Organization, there's no amount of alcohol considered safe for health.
slides.imageAlt: A blood pressure monitor on a table

slides.myth: A little alcohol relaxes you and improves performance.
slides.fact: A small amount of alcohol can reduce shyness for some people, but it does the opposite in the body: it can weaken erections and sensation. The more you drink, the clearer this effect becomes.
slides.imageAlt: Iced herbal tea with mint in a plain glass

quiz.question: How does alcohol affect sleep?
options: It can break up sleep in the second half of the night
It doesn't affect it at all
quiz.explain: Although alcohol makes falling asleep easier, it lowers sleep quality and can increase night-time waking.

slides.imageAlt: A man stretching in bed in the morning

slides.title: Take a look at the Alcohol-Free Camp
slides.text: If you want to cut down on alcohol or take a break for a while, the Alcohol-Free Camp offers a step-by-step plan. Taking a look doesn't commit you to anything.
slides.imageAlt: A road stretching through the countryside at sunrise and someone running

items: In the short term, alcohol can disrupt erections and sleep.
In the long term it affects blood pressure, blood vessels and hormone balance.
Cutting down or taking a break is good for both sleep and sexual health.

sources.title: NHS – Erection problems (erectile dysfunction)

WHO – Alcohol fact sheet

slides.title: Sleep and testosterone
slides.text: In men, a large part of daily testosterone release happens during sleep. That's why regular, sufficient sleep is a natural part of hormone balance.
slides.imageAlt: The moon in a blue night sky

slides.title: The effect of short sleep
slides.text: In a small study of healthy young men, sleeping about 5 hours a night for a week lowered daytime testosterone levels by about 10–15%. It's a single small study, but it shows how important sleep is.
slides.imageAlt: An alarm clock standing on a wooden floor

slides.text: The American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends that adults sleep at least 7 hours a night. Regularly sleeping less than 7 hours has been linked to weight gain, high blood pressure and heart disease.
slides.imageAlt: A plain, made bed in morning light

quiz.question: What happened to testosterone in the one-week short-sleep study?
quiz.explain: Although the study was small, the result shows how important sleep is for hormone balance. At least 7 hours of sleep is recommended for adults.

slides.imageAlt: A cup of coffee by a window

slides.title: Fix your bedtime tonight
slides.text: This week, try going to bed at the same time every night and make room for 7–8 hours of sleep. Set a reminder on your phone for 30 minutes before bedtime.
slides.imageAlt: A bedside lamp and an open notebook

items: A large part of testosterone is released during sleep.
Even a week of short sleep can lower testosterone.
The target for adults: at least 7 hours a night, at regular times.

sources.title: Leproult R, Van Cauter E (2011) – Effect of 1 week of sleep restriction on testosterone levels in young healthy men. JAMA 305
AASM & Sleep Research Society (2015) – Recommended amount of sleep for a healthy adult
NHS – How to get to sleep

title: An evening routine for better sleep

slides.title: Get up at the same time every day
slides.text: Getting up at the same time every day, weekends included, sets your body clock. Getting daylight in the morning also helps sleep come more easily in the evening.
slides.imageAlt: A hand opening the curtain in the morning sun

slides.title: Dim the lights and screens
slides.text: In the hour before bed, dim the lights and step away from screens. Reading a book, a warm shower or light stretching tell your body the day is over. Avoid caffeine in the evening too.
slides.imageAlt: Hands holding an open book in dim light

slides.title: If you can't sleep, get up
slides.text: If you can't sleep after about 20 minutes in bed, get up and do something calm in dim light. Go back when you feel sleepy. That way your brain pairs the bed with sleep, not with tossing and turning awake.
slides.imageAlt: A steaming kettle and a cup in a dim kitchen

slides.text: Experts recommend at least 7 hours of sleep a night for adults. A regular evening routine makes it easier to fall asleep and wake up refreshed.
slides.imageAlt: A shower and a bathrobe on a hook in a plain bathroom

quiz.question: What should you do if you can't sleep for a long time in bed?
options: Get up and do something calm in dim light
quiz.explain: Screen light and looking at the clock increase wakefulness. Taking a short break and going back to bed when you feel sleepy works better.

slides.imageAlt: A blanket and a book on an armchair

slides.title: 10 minutes of mind unload
slides.text: Writing down what's on your mind before bed can calm it. Try the mind unload exercise in the app this evening.
slides.imageAlt: An open notebook and pens under an evening lamp

items: Get up at the same time every day; get daylight in the morning.
Before bed, cut down on light, screens and caffeine.
If you can't sleep in 20 minutes, get up and go back when you're sleepy.

sources.title: NHS – How to get to sleep
AASM & Sleep Research Society (2015) – Recommended amount of sleep for a healthy adult

title: Getting up at night to urinate

slides.title: Getting up at night to urinate
slides.text: Waking up from sleep to urinate is called nocturia. It becomes more frequent with age and is very common. Getting up once a night is usually not a problem; twice or more can break up your sleep.
slides.imageAlt: A corridor with a night light on

slides.title: Adjust your evening fluids
slides.text: Drink enough during the day, but cut down on fluids in the 2 hours before bed. Avoid coffee, tea and alcohol in the evening; they can increase the amount of urine. Make going to the toilet just before bed a habit.
slides.imageAlt: A glass of water and a grapefruit on a table in the evening

slides.text: Fluid that collects in the legs during the day returns to the circulation when you lie down and can be passed as urine at night. That's why resting with your legs raised for a while in the evening can help. Loud snoring and pauses in breathing during sleep can also be linked to getting up at night to urinate.
slides.imageAlt: Feet in socks resting on a cushion on a sofa

quiz.question: What helps most in the 2 hours before bed?
options: Cutting down on fluids and avoiding caffeine
Putting off going to the toilet
quiz.explain: Cutting down on fluids and caffeine in the evening reduces the urine produced at night. Going to the toilet before bed helps too.

slides.imageAlt: A clock on the wall in evening light

slides.title: Evening fluid reminder
slides.text: Set a reminder on your phone for 2 hours before bedtime: “Today's last big glass.” For a week, note how many times you get up at night.
slides.imageAlt: A lit lamp and a phone on a bedside table

items: If you get up more than twice a night and it disrupts your sleep
If there's blood in your urine, burning or a fever
If you're very thirsty and urinate a lot
If loud snoring or pauses in breathing during sleep have been noticed
slides.imageAlt: A doctor's hands fitting a pulse oximeter on a finger

items: Getting up at night to urinate is common; twice or more can break up sleep.
Cut down on fluids and caffeine in the 2 hours before bed.
Swollen legs and snoring may play a part too; talk to a doctor.

sources.title: European Association of Urology (patient information) – Self-management of nocturia symptoms
Oxford Health NHS – Understanding nocturia
NHS – Urinary incontinence

title: How does stress feel in the body?

slides.title: Fight or flight
slides.text: When you sense danger, the body releases adrenaline and cortisol: your heart speeds up, you breathe faster and your muscles tense. This response, useful in short-term danger, wears the body out when stress is constant.
slides.imageAlt: Cars waiting in traffic in evening light

slides.title: Tense muscles
slides.text: Long-lasting stress keeps the muscles on constant alert; the neck, shoulders and jaw are where it's felt most. The pelvic floor can tense up too. A constantly tense pelvic floor can contribute to pain and to difficulties in the toilet or with sexual function.
slides.imageAlt: A man stretching his neck with his hands behind his head

slides.title: Relaxing is a skill too
slides.text: Learning to let a muscle go matters as much as squeezing it. Breathing exercises, the body scan and regular movement reduce muscle tension. The relaxation moments in your workouts are part of this skill too.
slides.imageAlt: A man lying on the grass with his eyes closed

slides.myth: Stress only happens in your head.
slides.fact: Stress is felt in the body too: muscle tension, headaches, digestive problems and poor sleep are common signs. The American Psychological Association notes that relaxation techniques reduce muscle tension.
slides.imageAlt: A man thinking at a laptop, from behind

quiz.question: How does long-lasting stress affect the muscles?
options: It can keep them constantly tense
It doesn't affect it at all
quiz.explain: Short-term stress tenses the muscles for a moment and then releases them. When stress continues, the muscles stay on alert; this can lead to pain and fatigue.

slides.imageAlt: Two ropes hanging side by side

slides.title: Do a body scan
slides.text: Take a few minutes and scan your body from head to toe: notice where there's tension and let it go as you breathe out.
slides.imageAlt: A man lying on his back on the floor with his eyes closed

items: The stress response tenses the muscles; constant stress wears the body out.
The pelvic floor can tense up with stress too.
Relaxing is as important a skill as squeezing.

sources.title: American Psychological Association – Stress effects on the body
NHS – Tips to reduce stress

slides.title: Postpone the worry
slides.text: When a worry comes to mind during the day, don't try to solve it right away. Jot it down briefly and tell yourself: “I'll think about this in my worry time.” Then go back to what you were doing.
slides.imageAlt: A man holding a small notebook in front of his shirt

slides.title: Worry time
slides.text: Every day at the same time, at least a few hours before bed, set aside 15 minutes. Read what you noted. Some will no longer seem important; for the rest, think about whether there's a step you can take.
slides.imageAlt: A small clock on a notebook

slides.title: Can it be solved?
slides.text: Split your worries in two: the ones you can do something about and the “what if” kind of assumptions. For the first, plan a small step; notice the second and let it go. When time is up, close the notebook.
slides.imageAlt: A path splitting in two in the countryside

slides.text: This technique comes from cognitive behavioural therapy and is among the NHS's self-help suggestions. With regular practice, you may notice you get caught up in worries less during the day.
slides.imageAlt: An open book and a pen

quiz.question: What do you do when a worry comes during the day?
options: I note it down and leave it for worry time
I think about it for hours straight away
I ignore it and try to suppress it
quiz.explain: Trying to suppress a worry often makes it stronger; thinking about it for hours is exhausting too. Postponing gives the worry a place while protecting your day from it.

slides.imageAlt: A hand taking notes in a notebook next to a phone

slides.title: Set a worry time for tomorrow
slides.text: Choose a 15-minute worry time for tomorrow and put it in your calendar; not close to bedtime. Collect the worries that come during the day in one note.
slides.imageAlt: A hand writing in a planner, the writing unreadable

items: Note down the worry that comes and postpone it to worry time.
Set aside 15 minutes at the same time every day; well before bed.
Plan a step for what can be solved; notice the assumption and let it go.

sources.title: NHS Every Mind Matters – Tackling your worries
Oxford Health NHS – Set aside worry time
NHS – Tips to reduce stress

slides.title: Attention to the present
slides.text: Mindfulness means paying attention, without judgement, to what's happening right now: your thoughts, feelings, sounds and the sensations in your body. It isn't anything mystical; it's an attention exercise you can practise regularly.
slides.imageAlt: A single drop of water on a leaf, close-up

slides.title: When the mind wanders
slides.text: During practice your mind will drift elsewhere; that's normal and not a mistake. As soon as you notice, gently bring your attention back to your breath. Every return is the exercise itself.
slides.imageAlt: White clouds passing in a blue sky

slides.title: A 1-minute try
slides.text: Sit comfortably, close your eyes or look at one spot. Notice your breath going in and out through your nose. For one minute, just watch without counting or changing it. If your attention drifts, come back to the breath.
slides.imageAlt: A man sitting on a chair with his eyes closed

slides.myth: For mindfulness, you have to empty your head completely.
slides.fact: The aim isn't to stop thoughts but to notice them and come back to the breath without getting pulled in. Thoughts coming is a natural part of the practice.
slides.imageAlt: A wavy water surface shining in the light

quiz.question: What do you do if your mind wanders during practice?
options: I notice it and gently come back to the breath
I think I've failed and give up
I try to force my thoughts to stop
quiz.explain: The mind wanders; what matters is noticing and coming back. Trying to force it to stop increases tension.

slides.imageAlt: A gentle wave breaking on the beach

slides.title: 1 minute of attention to the breath
slides.text: Take a minute now and pay attention to your breath. If you like, start with the breathing exercise in the app.
slides.imageAlt: A man sipping his coffee outdoors, side view

items: Mindfulness is non-judgemental attention to the present.
The mind wanders; noticing and gently coming back is the practice itself.
Even starting with one minute a day is a good enough step.

sources.title: NHS – Mindfulness
NCCIH – Meditation and mindfulness: what you need to know

slides.title: How much movement?
slides.text: The World Health Organization recommends 150–300 minutes of moderate movement a week for adults: brisk walking, cycling or swimming, for example. On top of this, strength training should be done on at least 2 days a week.
slides.imageAlt: A man walking along a flowery path in a park, from behind

slides.title: Break up long sitting
slides.text: Staying inactive for long periods is bad for your health. Get up for a few minutes every hour, walk or stretch. Even a little movement is better than none.
slides.imageAlt: A man stretching his arms while sitting on a bench with his laptop

slides.title: Benefits for blood vessels and erections
slides.text: Regular movement helps regulate blood pressure and blood sugar and supports the flexibility of your blood vessels. In a study of obese men, weight loss and movement improved sexual function in about a third of participants.
slides.imageAlt: A man cycling in the city

slides.myth: To get any benefit, I need to go to the gym every day.
slides.fact: Climbing stairs, walking briskly or a short routine at home count too. According to the World Health Organization, every move counts; even a little movement brings benefits.
slides.imageAlt: A foot climbing up bright steps

quiz.question: How much moderate movement a week does the World Health Organization recommend for adults?
quiz.explain: 150–300 minutes a week can be met with, for example, a walk of about 30 minutes a day. Strength training on 2 days a week is added to this.

slides.imageAlt: Running shoes on autumn leaves

slides.title: Pelvic Fitness: Beginner
slides.text: Start strength training with a small step: the Pelvic Fitness beginner routine takes about 7 minutes and works your hips, abs and pelvic floor together.
slides.imageAlt: An older man doing squats at home

items: 150–300 minutes of moderate movement a week and 2 days of strength.
Break up long sitting with a few minutes every hour.
Movement supports your blood vessels and sexual health.

sources.title: WHO (2020) – Guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour
WHO – Physical activity fact sheet
Esposito K et al. (2004) – Effect of lifestyle changes on erectile dysfunction in obese men: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA 291

title: Why do the hips and core matter?

slides.title: A team that works together
slides.text: The pelvic floor doesn't work alone; together with the deep abdominal muscles, the back muscles and the diaphragm, it forms the “box” of the core. When one contracts, the others usually join in.
slides.imageAlt: A rowing team on the water at sunset, from a distance

slides.title: The role of the hips
slides.text: The hip muscles keep the pelvis balanced; they support the body when walking, climbing stairs and lifting. Strong hip and abdominal muscles share the load on the pelvic floor.
slides.imageAlt: A man climbing stairs, side view

slides.title: Control and posture
slides.text: A strong core that works in harmony can support bladder control and posture when coughing or lifting. Moves like the bridge, bird-dog and plank work these muscles together.
slides.imageAlt: A man walking with good posture carrying boxes

slides.text: Research shows that when the pelvic floor contracts, the deep abdominal muscles work along with it. That's why gently drawing in your belly during exercises, without holding your breath, also supports the pelvic floor.
slides.imageAlt: A man doing a forearm plank on a mat

quiz.question: Which muscles does the pelvic floor work with?
options: The deep abdominal and back muscles, and the diaphragm
quiz.explain: These muscles work like a team and manage the pressure inside the abdomen together. That's why core exercises also help the pelvic floor.

slides.imageAlt: Stones balanced on top of pebbles

slides.title: Pelvic Fitness routine
slides.text: Today, try a short routine of moves that work the core together, like the bridge and the bird-dog.
slides.imageAlt: A man lying on his back on a mat at home, raising his legs

items: The pelvic floor works together with the abs, back and diaphragm.
Strong hip and abdominal muscles share the pelvic floor's load.
The bridge, bird-dog and plank strengthen this team together.

sources.title: North Bristol NHS Trust – Pelvic floor exercises for men
Neumann P, Gill V (2002) – Pelvic floor and abdominal muscle interaction: EMG activity and intra-abdominal pressure. Int Urogynecol J 13
WHO – Physical activity fact sheet

slides.title: Saddle pressure
slides.text: When cycling, part of your weight rests on the perineum (between the anus and testicles), where nerves and blood vessels pass. On long rides this pressure can cause numbness or tingling.
slides.imageAlt: A bicycle saddle, close-up

slides.title: Precautions
slides.text: Choose a saddle that suits you, with a cut-out or a wider shape. Adjust the saddle height and angle; don't keep the handlebars much lower than the saddle. Stand on the pedals now and then while riding to relieve the pressure.
slides.imageAlt: Hands checking a bicycle on the grass

slides.fact: Research shows that men who cycle regularly don't have worse erectile function than those who don't. To reduce numbness, the right saddle, the right setup and short breaks matter.
slides.imageAlt: Someone cycling along a road through the countryside, from a distance

quiz.question: In one study, what reduced genital numbness?
options: Standing on the pedals for part of the ride
Keeping the handlebars much lower than the saddle
quiz.explain: Those who stood on the pedals for more than 20% of the ride had less numbness. Having the handlebars lower than the saddle increased numbness.

slides.imageAlt: A blue bicycle saddle, close-up

slides.title: Stand up every 10 minutes when riding
slides.text: On your next ride, stand on the pedals about every 10 minutes to relieve the pressure for a few seconds. Notice whether the numbness decreases.
slides.imageAlt: The legs of a cyclist pedalling

items: If numbness is frequent or doesn't go away after riding (take a break from cycling meanwhile)
If you've noticed a new problem with erections
If there's pain, swelling or a sore in the perineal area
If you have straining or burning when urinating
slides.imageAlt: A doctor working at their desk in a bright practice

items: Long saddle pressure can cause numbness in the perineal area.
A suitable saddle, the right setup and standing up now and then matter.
Cycling alone doesn't cause erection problems; taking precautions is enough.

sources.title: SMSNA – Is cycling a risk factor for erectile dysfunction?
Awad MA et al. (2018) – Erectile and urinary function in men who cycle. Journal of Urology

slides.title: Smoking and blood vessels
slides.text: The substances in cigarettes damage the inner lining of blood vessels and narrow them. Because erections depend on healthy blood flow, smokers have a higher risk of erection problems; the more they smoke, the higher the risk.
slides.imageAlt: Thin tree branches against the sky

slides.title: What changes when you quit?
slides.text: When you quit, blood vessel function starts to recover over time: in the first hours the carbon monoxide in your blood drops, and within weeks circulation and breathing improve. In one study, erectile function improved after a year in about a quarter of the men who quit.
slides.imageAlt: A window with a sheer curtain opening onto a garden

slides.myth: I've smoked for years; quitting won't help now.
slides.fact: Quitting helps at any age. According to the World Health Organization, the gains start in the first hours and grow over the years. Quitting while young and while the problem is mild makes more of a difference for erections.
slides.imageAlt: An older man walking in a park with a cane in autumn, from behind

quiz.question: What happens to blood vessel health when you quit smoking?
options: It starts to recover over time
quiz.explain: Blood vessels start to repair themselves after you quit. That's why the benefits of quitting can show in both the heart and erections.

slides.imageAlt: A man in a meadow opening his arms and taking a deep breath, from behind

slides.title: Smoke-Free Camp assessment
slides.text: If you're thinking about quitting, the Smoke-Free Camp prepares a plan for you with a short assessment. You can take a look even if you don't feel ready.
slides.imageAlt: A trail starting in a forest in morning light

items: If erection problems keep coming back
If you have chest pain, shortness of breath or a cough that won't go away
If withdrawal symptoms are really hard while quitting (ALO 171 in Türkiye or your local quitline can also help)
If you have heart disease, diabetes or high blood pressure, about medicines that support quitting
slides.imageAlt: A results sheet in a doctor's hand

items: Smoking narrows blood vessels and increases the risk of erection problems.
When you quit, blood vessel function recovers over time.
Quitting helps at any age; getting support makes it easier.
